newsitem.title: USA: Judge orders Detroit newspapers to rehire strikers.
newsitem.headline: Judge orders Detroit newspapers to rehire strikers.

text.p: An administrative law judge ordered Detroit's two newspapers to give 2,000 striking workers their jobs back after a bitter, nearly two-year-old labour clash.

Judge Thomas Wilks, in a decision released Friday from the National Labour Relations Board in Washington, said the strike against the Detroit News and Detroit Free Press was in response to unfair labour practices by the papers.
The unions hailed the decision as a victory, while the newspapers said they were likely to appeal the decision.

The decision means that the approximately 1,500 replacement reporters, distribution and production workers hired by the papers may be fired, if necessary, to make room for the returning strikers, Wilks said in his ruling.

Wilks' decision upholds an earlier complaint from the regional NLRB director in Detroit that the newspapers and their joint operating agency, Detroit Newspapers Inc., did not bargain in good faith with the six striking unions.
The News is owned by Gannett Co. Inc., while Knight-Ridder Inc. owns the Free Press. The papers are editorially independent but jointly published by Detroit Newspapers.

Because of advance planning and tight security measures, the papers have published every day since the strike began on July 13, 1995. The walkout is regarded as one of the longest newspaper strikes to hit a major metropolitan area.
Union leaders called the ruling a major victory.

"It has been a long haul, but this is a sign that we are turning the corner and that we are going to win justice and contracts," said Al Derey, chairman of the Metropolitan Council of Newspaper Unions, which represents the unions.

The newspapers said their attorneys were reviewing the 120-page opinion and were likely to appeal to the NLRB. If that fails, the papers can take their case to the U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, and the U.S. Supreme Court, a process that analysts have said could take years.
Detroit Newspapers Chief Executive Officer Frank Vega called Wilks' ruling a split decision because he found against the unions on some matters.
"The decision is no surprise. We did not expect to win the entire case at this level, particulary before a judge appointed by the Labour Board," he said.

The unions set the stage for worker reinstatement in February by making an unconditional offer to return to work. At the time, they said the newspapers could be liable for back pay of $1 million a year if they rejected the offer and were found to have committed unfair labour practices.
Since the sometimes violent strike began, more than 400 strikers have returned to work. The papers said they had eliminated about 600 jobs through efficiencies.
Although they have continued to publish, circulation fell 30 percent and advertising was down 15 percent to 20 percent as of February.
